'''Philip Louis Felgner''' (born 7 February 1950) is an American biochemist and immunologist known for his work on [[lipofection]] technology and nucleic acid delivery systems.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Felgner |first1=P L |last2=Gadek |first2=T R |last3=Holm |first3=M |last4=Roman |first4=R |last5=Chan |first5=H W |last6=Wenz |first6=M |last7=Northrop |first7=J P |last8=Ringold |first8=G M |last9=Danielsen |first9=M |date=November 1987 |title=Lipofection: a highly efficient, lipid-mediated DNA-transfection procedure. |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=84 |issue=21 |pages=7413–7417 |doi=10.1073/pnas.84.21.7413 |doi-access=free |issn=0027-8424 |pmid=2823261|pmc=299306 |bibcode=1987PNAS...84.7413F }}</ref> His research has focused on the development of lipid-based methods for introducing nucleic acids into cells and their applications in gene delivery and vaccination. He is currently a Professor of Physiology & Biophysics at the [[University of California, Irvine]] (UCI), where he serves as Director of the UCI Vaccine Research & Development Center and the Protein Microarray Laboratory and Training Facility.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Phil Felgner, PhD, joins Physiology & Biophysics {{!}} Department of Physiology and Biophysics {{!}} School of Medicine {{!}} University of California, Irvine |url=https://www.physiology.uci.edu/New%20Faculty/Phil%20Felgner.asp |access-date=2024-10-16 |website=www.physiology.uci.edu}}</ref>

Felgner's work on cationic lipid-based nucleic acid transfection and the demonstration that direct injection of nucleic acids can result in ''[[in vivo]]'' protein expression contributed to the development of [[lipid nanoparticle]] delivery systems and informed subsequent work on [[DNA vaccine]]s and [[mRNA vaccine]]s.

==Early life and education==
Felgner was born and raised in [[Frankenmuth, Michigan]], a small farming community with German heritage. He developed an early interest in science during a period of rapid technological advancement in the United States.

In 1972, he graduated in biochemistry from [[Michigan State University]], earning his master's degree in 1975 and his Ph.D. in 1978. He conducted postdoctoral research at the [[University of Virginia]], where he studied [[liposome]]s—lipid-based structures investigated for their potential use in drug delivery.<ref>[https://www.faculty.uci.edu/profile.cfm?faculty_id=5085 Philip L. Felgner UCI profile]</ref>

==Career and research==

===Development of lipofection technology===
While working at [[Syntex]] in the mid-1980s, Felgner helped pioneer the use of synthetic cationic lipids to facilitate the delivery of nucleic acids into cells.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Felgner |first1=P L |last2=Gadek |first2=T R |last3=Holm |first3=M |last4=Roman |first4=R |last5=Chan |first5=H W |last6=Wenz |first6=M |last7=Northrop |first7=J P |last8=Ringold |first8=G M |last9=Danielsen |first9=M |date=November 1987 |title=Lipofection: a highly efficient, lipid-mediated DNA-transfection procedure. |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=84 |issue=21 |pages=7413–7417 |doi=10.1073/pnas.84.21.7413 |doi-access=free |pmc=299306 |pmid=2823261|bibcode=1987PNAS...84.7413F }}</ref> This work introduced cationic lipid-based transfection reagents and contributed to the development of synthetic non-viral [[gene delivery]] methods. These approaches became widely used tools in molecular and cellular biology.

At the [[Salk Institute for Biological Studies]] in [[San Diego]], [[California]], he further investigated RNA transfection in a range of model systems, with results published in 1989.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Malone |first1=R W |last2=Felgner |first2=P L |last3=Verma |first3=I M |date=August 1989 |title=Cationic liposome-mediated RNA transfection. |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=86 |issue=16 |pages=6077–6081 |doi=10.1073/pnas.86.16.6077 |doi-access=free |pmc=297778 |pmid=2762315|bibcode=1989PNAS...86.6077M }}</ref>

===Foundation of DNA and RNA vaccination===
In 1990, while working at [[Vical|Vical Inc.]], a company he founded, Felgner collaborated with researchers at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] to demonstrate that injection of [[plasmid DNA]] (pDNA) and [[mRNA]] into mouse skeletal muscle could result in protein expression.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wolff |first1=Jon A. |last2=Malone |first2=Robert W. |last3=Williams |first3=Phillip |last4=Chong |first4=Wang |last5=Acsadi |first5=Gyula |last6=Jani |first6=Agnes |last7=Felgner |first7=Philip L. |date=1990-03-23 |title=Direct Gene Transfer into Mouse Muscle in Vivo |url=https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.1690918 |journal=Science |volume=247 |issue=4949 |pages=1465–1468 |doi=10.1126/science.1690918|pmid=1690918 |bibcode=1990Sci...247.1465W |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cullis |first1=P. R. |last2=Felgner |first2=P. L. |date=September 2024 |title=The 60-year evolution of lipid nanoparticles for nucleic acid delivery |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41573-024-00977-6 |journal=Nature Reviews Drug Discovery |volume=23 |issue=9 |pages=709–722 |doi=10.1038/s41573-024-00977-6 |pmid=38965378 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> This study provided early evidence that direct administration of nucleic acids could produce proteins ''[[in vivo]]'', an approach later explored in [[gene therapy]] and vaccine development. Subsequent research has identified this work as part of the early development of [[mRNA vaccine]] technologies.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dolgin |first=Elie |date=2021-09-14 |title=The tangled history of mRNA vaccines |journal=Nature |volume=597 |issue=7876 |pages=318–324 |doi=10.1038/d41586-021-02483-w|pmid=34522017 }}</ref>

During the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], mRNA vaccine platforms developed by companies such as [[BioNTech]] and [[Moderna]] utilized lipid nanoparticle delivery systems related to earlier work in the field.

===Academic career and protein microarray technology===
In 2002, Felgner joined the faculty at UC Irvine. In addition to his work on lipid-based delivery systems, he developed large-scale [[protein microarray]] technologies for studying immune responses. His laboratory has generated extensive collections of cloned [[plasmid]]s and corresponding protein arrays used to analyze antibody responses to infectious diseases.

These arrays have been applied to tens of thousands of [[Blood serum|sera]] samples from infected, vaccinated, and uninfected individuals, enabling the identification of immunologically relevant [[antigen]]s and patterns of [[immune system]] response.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, his laboratory analyzed thousands of specimens to study immune responses to infection and vaccination. The group also developed microarray-based tools to assess exposure to SARS-CoV-2 and its [[Variant of concern|variants]].

Felgner has collaborated with researchers and clinicians across multiple institutions on studies related to vaccine development, immune profiling, and infectious disease diagnostics.

==Impact and recognition==
As of 2022, Felgner has published more than 300 [[peer-reviewed]] papers that have been cited over 58,000 times.<ref>{{Cite web |last=taylorrr |date=2022-12-13 |title=Phil Felgner named Fellow by National Academy of Inventors |url=https://immunology.uci.edu/2022/12/12/phil-felgner-named-fellow-by-national-academy-of-inventors/ |access-date=2024-10-16 |website=Institute for Immunology }}</ref> He holds numerous U.S. and international patents related to gene delivery and biotechnology.

In 2023, his work on cationic lipid-based delivery systems was referenced in background materials associated with the [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2023]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2023 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2023/advanced-information/ |access-date=2024-10-16 |website=NobelPrize.org}}</ref>

==Honors and awards==
Felgner has received numerous prestigious honors recognizing his contributions to science and medicine:

* '''[[Princess of Asturias Awards]] for Technical and Scientific Research''' (2021) – awarded along with [[Katalin Karikó]], [[Drew Weissman]], [[Uğur Şahin]], [[Özlem Türeci]], [[Derrick Rossi]], and [[Sarah Gilbert]] for contributions to designing COVID-19 vaccines<ref>{{cite web|title=Katalin Karikó, Drew Weissman, Philip Felgner, Uğur Şahin, Özlem Türeci, Derrick Rossi, and Sarah Gilbert, Princess of Asturias Award for Technical and Scientific Research 2021|publisher=Princess of Asturias Foundation|url=https://www.fpa.es/en/princess-of-asturias-awards/laureates/2021-katalin-kariko-drew-weissman-philip-felgner-ugur-sahin-ozlem-tureci-derrick-rossi-and-sarah-gilbert.html|date=23 June 2021}}</ref>
* '''[[Robert Koch Prize]]''' (2022) – one of the most prestigious honors in infectious disease research and microbiology, often considered a stepping-stone to eventual [[Nobel Prize]] recognition, awarded for his fundamental contributions to the development of [[lipofection]] technology<ref>{{Cite web |title=UCI professor wins prestigious Robert Koch prize {{!}} UCI Health {{!}} Orange County, CA |url=https://www.ucihealth.org/news/2022/04/uci-professor-wins-prestigious-robert-koch-prize |access-date=2024-10-16 |website=www.ucihealth.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Robert Koch Award |url=https://www.robert-koch-stiftung.de/en/awards/robert-koch-award |access-date=2024-10-16 |website=www.robert-koch-stiftung.de |language=en-en}}</ref>
* '''A.D. Bangham FRS Life Achievement Award''' (2022) – named in honor of Dr. [[Alec Douglas Bangham]], known as the father of liposomes<ref>{{Cite web |title=LRD 2022: Awards – NMIN – Nanomedicines Innovation Network |url=https://www.nanomedicines.ca/lrd-2022-awards/ |access-date=2025-01-03 |language=en-CA}}</ref>
* '''[[National Academy of Inventors]] Fellow''' (2022)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fellows |url=https://academyofinventors.org/search-fellows/ |access-date=2024-10-16 |website=NAI |language=en-US}}</ref>
* Multiple lifetime achievement awards from leading scientific organizations
